opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most interesting open questions right now. Math and coding are the easy cases because you have a crisp verifier: either the unit tests pass or they don't, either you got the right number or you didn't. That clean reward signal is a big part of why we've seen such rapid progress there with reinforcement learning.

But I'm actually more optimistic than a lot of people about extending this to fuzzier domains. There's a general asymmetry where verifying something is often much easier than generating it. Even if a model can't write a great essay or a great legal brief, it can frequently tell you which of two essays is better, or point out that an argument has a hole in it. And you can make the grading much more reliable by breaking it down. Instead of asking "is this a good answer?", you give the model a rubric with specific, checkable criteria. Did it address the counterargument? Did it cite the relevant precedent? Is the claim in paragraph three actually supported? Each of those individual judgments is far more tractable than one holistic score.

The obvious worry is reward hacking. If the grader has blind spots, the policy will find them. It'll learn to sound confident, write longer, use the vocabulary the grader likes, without actually being better. We see versions of that all the time. So you need things like ensembles of graders, graders that are stronger than the policy, periodic human spot-checks, and rubrics that keep getting refreshed so the model can't just overfit to one judge's quirks.

I'd also say a lot of seemingly fuzzy domains have more ground truth than people assume. Medicine has outcomes. Forecasting resolves eventually. Scientific claims can be checked against experiments or the literature. Even in writing, you can measure whether a reader actually understood the thing afterward. So I don't think of it as a binary between verifiable and unverifiable tasks. It's more of a spectrum of how expensive and noisy your signal is, and models grading models pushes a lot of things further toward the cheap, usable end of that spectrum.

r002.rationale: It discusses fuzzy domains and grader blind spots, but does not identify judgments requiring expertise or taste as a harder case.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most important questions right now, because the whole reason math and coding have moved so fast is that you have this crisp verifiable signal. The proof checks or it doesn't, the tests pass or they don't. And the question everyone's asking is whether that generalizes.

My honest take is that it generalizes more than people expect, but it's not free. The thing people underrate is that models are often much better at recognizing a good answer than at producing one. There's this generator-verifier gap. If you ask me to write a great essay on some topic, that's hard. If you hand me two essays and ask which is better, I can usually tell you, and I can tell you why. Models have that same asymmetry. So you can get surprisingly far using the model as the grader even in fuzzy domains like writing or legal reasoning or giving medical advice.

The catch is that the grader is now a learned thing with its own blind spots, and when you optimize hard against it, you find the blind spots. That's the classic reward hacking story. The policy learns that the grader likes answers that are longer, or more confident, or that use certain phrasings, and you get this drift away from what you actually wanted. In math, the hacking is bounded because there's ground truth at the end. In open-ended domains there's no ground truth to anchor to, so the grader has to be really robust.

What I think actually works is a few things stacked together. One is rubrics. Instead of asking "is this good," you decompose into "did it address the actual question, did it make any factual claims that are wrong, did it hedge appropriately," and the model is much more reliable at each of those narrow checks than at the holistic judgment. Two is giving the grader more compute than the policy. Let it think longer, let it look things up, let it run comparisons. Asymmetric effort helps a lot. And three, honestly, is still having humans in the loop at the top of the stack, calibrating the graders against a small set of really carefully labeled examples, because you need some ground truth somewhere.

The thing I find exciting from the interpretability side is that you can also sometimes look inside the grader and ask whether it's actually tracking the thing you care about or just some correlate. If the "this is a good answer" feature is really a "this sounds confident" feature, you'd want to know that before you train against it for a million steps.

So I'd say the frontier isn't whether models can grade beyond math and code. They clearly can to some degree. It's whether we can make that grading robust enough to optimize against, and that's a much harder bar.

r002.rationale: It discusses the difficulty of robust grading in open-ended domains, but does not identify judgments requiring expertise or taste as a harder case.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention difficulty finding human writers with a desired literary taste or an effort to teach models to write.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how much easier it is to recognize a good answer than to produce one. In math and coding, you often have something external you can check: does the proof hold up, or do the tests pass? In other domains, a model can still give useful feedback, but it’s harder to know whether it’s rewarding correctness or just something that sounds convincing.

Take an explanation of a scientific concept. You can ask whether it’s internally consistent, whether it addresses the question, and whether its claims follow from the evidence you’ve provided. Those are fairly concrete things to evaluate. Asking whether it’s a genuinely insightful explanation is much harder. The grader might prefer a familiar, polished answer over an unusual answer that’s actually better.

And that distinction matters a lot once you optimize against the grader. A model being reasonably good at comparing ordinary answers doesn’t necessarily mean it will keep making good judgments when another model is trained to exploit its preferences.

So I’m optimistic that grading can extend well beyond math and coding. But I’d want to break the task into specific criteria and check the grader against independent evidence or human judgment. Otherwise, you risk improving the score without improving the underlying capability.

r002.rationale: It says judging whether an explanation is genuinely insightful is much harder and warns that a grader may favor familiar polish over a better but unusual answer.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention difficulty finding human writers with a desired literary taste or an effort to teach models to write.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between being able to generate a good answer and being able to recognize one. In math and coding, we have these really convenient checks: does the proof work, do the tests pass? Outside those domains, there’s still a lot you can evaluate, but the signal gets noisier.

If you ask a model to critique an essay, it can often identify a contradiction, an unsupported claim, or a confusing explanation, even if it couldn’t have written a great essay itself. So I wouldn’t assume that everything without a programmatic verifier is inaccessible to reinforcement learning.

The question is whether the grader is tracking what we actually care about. Is it rewarding a better argument, or just a longer answer that sounds authoritative? And if you optimize against that grader hard enough, you’ll find its blind spots. Agreement between models doesn’t necessarily solve that, because they might share the same blind spots.

So I’m optimistic about using models to provide feedback beyond math and coding. But I’d want to distinguish improvements in the grader’s score from improvements that hold up when a person actually uses the answer.
